title: Trees: Complete OA Preparation Guide
subtitle: All Variations — BFS, Views, Construction, Height, Root-to-Leaf, Ancestors, BST, Tree DP, Serialize
author: Mayank Verma · IIIT Kottayam · Batch 2023–2027
overview: Every tree problem in OA rounds reduces to one of two templates. Recognize which one applies before writing any code.
coreConcept: **Template 1 — BFS (Level Order)** for anything where level information matters, and **Template 2 — DFS (recursive post-order / pre-order)** for anything where subtree information matters. Most "hard" tree problems are one of these two skeletons with a different value collected at each node.

foundationTemplates.label: Universal BFS Template
Universal DFS Template

triggerWords: **Use BFS when:** level info matters, view from a direction, width, distance between nodes.
**Use DFS when:** height, path sums, subtree properties, LCA, construction from traversals.
**Use both when:** Distance-K (parent map via DFS, then BFS from target).

foundationTricks: **Level snapshot**: Always `int size = queue.size()` BEFORE the inner loop.
**Return vs global**: DFS often needs a return value for the parent AND updates a global answer. These are usually different values.
**Null base case matters**: For height: `null -> 0`. For path sum: `null -> Integer.MIN_VALUE`. Choose carefully.
**BST property**: In a BST, inorder traversal gives a sorted sequence. Many BST problems reduce to inorder traversal problems.
**Index scheme**: Root=1, left child of node i = 2i, right = 2i+1. Used for width and completeness.
**Horizontal Distance (HD)**: Root=0, left child = parent.HD - 1, right = parent.HD + 1. Used for views.
**Bitmask for palindrome paths**: XOR a bitmask of digits seen; path is pseudo-palindromic if at most one bit is set.
commonMistakes: **BFS: missing size snapshot.** Not capturing `int size = queue.size()` before the inner loop causes nodes from different levels to be mixed. Most common BFS bug.
**Null root.** Always check `if (root == null)` before offering to a queue or starting recursion that accesses node fields.
**Integer overflow in width.** Node indices grow as 2^n. Use `long` and normalize at each level.
**Min depth null child trap.** A node with one null child is NOT a leaf. `1 + min(0, right)` would incorrectly return 1. Handle one-sided nodes explicitly.
**BST validation: only checking immediate children.** A right subtree node can be less than the root's ancestor. Pass valid [min, max] ranges, not just parent value.
**LCA: returning early.** If you find p or q and return immediately, you miss the case where q is a descendant of p (the answer should be p itself). The standard LCA code handles this correctly.
**Tree DP: not clipping negative arms.** In max path sum, a negative subtree contribution should be ignored (clip to 0). Forgetting `Math.max(0, dfs(...))` gives wrong answers.
**Postorder in LC 979.** Returning wrong excess (forgetting to subtract 1 for the current node's own requirement).
**Zigzag: reversing enqueue order.** Never change enqueue order. Only change the collection (insertion) direction.
**Serialize: not handling null root.** `deserialize("")` or `deserialize("N")` should return null, not throw.
**Recover BST: only finding one inversion.** There are two inversions in the inorder sequence. First bad node is `prev` at first inversion; second bad node is `current` at last inversion.
**Vertical Order: same (row, col) tie-breaking.** LC 987 requires sorting by value within same position. Forgetting the PriorityQueue gives wrong order.
interviewTips: **State the template first.** For any tree problem, say: "I'll use BFS/DFS with..." before coding. This signals pattern recognition immediately.
**Two-return-value DFS.** When a DFS needs to pass different information to the parent vs. update a global, be explicit: "DFS returns X to parent, and updates global Y at each node."
**BST ⇒ inorder = sorted.** Whenever you see a BST problem, immediately ask: does this reduce to an inorder traversal?
**Tree DP state table.** Before coding LC 337, 968-style problems, write a small table: what does DFS return? What are the state transitions? This prevents bugs.
**Top vs Bottom vs Vertical.** Be ready to explain: Top View = HD, first BFS visit. Bottom View = HD, last BFS visit. Vertical = ALL visits per (HD, depth), sorted by value.
**Overflow in width.** Mention normalization proactively. This shows senior-level awareness.
**Cameras greedy.** For LC 968, explain the greedy insight: never place a camera at a leaf (wasteful — it covers only itself and parent but not grandparent). This justifies the bottom-up approach.
**Serialize choice.** Preorder + nulls is simplest for general trees. BST saves space by exploiting BST property (no nulls needed).
**Construction: always build the index map.** For LC 105/106, always use a HashMap for inorder lookup. O(n) vs O(n^2) difference, and interviewers will ask about it.
**Distance-K: state the two phases clearly.** Phase 1: build parent map. Phase 2: BFS from target treating tree as undirected. Interviewers sometimes follow up with the DFS alternative.

variations.name: Standard Level Order (BFS)
variations.coreIdea: All problems here share the BFS template. The only variation is *what you collect* per level and whether you track horizontal distance or node index.

boxes.body: BFS processes nodes FIFO, which is exactly left-to-right within a level. The inner `for` loop bounded by `size` ensures exactly one level per outer iteration.

solved.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal

boxes.body: BFS processes nodes FIFO, which is exactly left-to-right within a level. The inner `for` loop bounded by `size` ensures exactly one level per outer iteration.
Snapshot the queue size before the inner loop. Poll exactly `size` nodes, collect their values, enqueue their children. Each node enters and exits the queue once.

complexity.spaceNote: w = max level width (up to O(n) for last level of perfect tree)

solved.title: Deepest Leaves Sum

boxes.body: BFS, reset a running `levelSum` at each level. After the loop, `levelSum` holds the deepest level's sum.

solved.title: Even Odd Tree
solved.statement: Even-indexed levels must have strictly increasing odd values; odd-indexed levels must have strictly decreasing even values. Return true if the tree satisfies this.

boxes.body: Track level index. Two checks per node: parity of value, and strict monotonicity relative to previous node on same level.

solved.title: Add One Row to Tree
solved.statement: Insert a row of nodes with value `val` at depth `depth`. Original subtrees become left/right children of new nodes. If depth == 1, new node becomes root.

boxes.body: BFS to level (depth-1). For each node there, insert two new nodes between it and its existing children.

variations.name: Zigzag Level Order
variations.coreIdea: Same BFS skeleton as level order; only the insertion direction into the per-level list alternates.

boxes.body: Never change the enqueue order. Only change the *insertion direction* into the output list using `addFirst`/`addLast` on a `LinkedList`.

solved.title: Reverse Odd Levels of Binary Tree
solved.statement: Given a *perfect* binary tree, reverse the node values at every odd-indexed level. Return the modified root.

boxes.body: BFS, collect all nodes at each level. When the level index is odd, swap values from both ends inward (two-pointer on the collected list). Swap values, not pointers.

variations.name: Tree Views (Side, Top, Bottom, Vertical)
variations.coreIdea:
All view problems are BFS with a different collection rule. Side views collect one node per level; top/bottom views key by horizontal distance (HD); vertical order keeps every node grouped by column.

**HD rule:** Root=0, left child = HD-1, right child = HD+1. Use `TreeMap<HD, value>` for sorted column output.
**Top View:** `putIfAbsent` — only first (topmost) BFS visit per HD.
**Bottom View:** `put` — last BFS visit per HD wins.

boxes.body: Right Side View collects the last node of each level (`i == size - 1`); Bottom Left Value collects the first node of each level (`i == 0`) and keeps the last one recorded.

solved.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
solved.statement: Return the values of nodes visible from the right side, one per level top to bottom.

boxes.body: BFS. At each level, collect the last node (`i == size - 1`). That is the only node visible from the right.

complexity.space: O(h) for result; O(w) for queue

solved.title: Find Bottom Left Tree Value
solved.statement: Find the leftmost value in the last row of the binary tree.

boxes.body: BFS. At each level, record the first node's value (`i == 0`). After BFS, the last recorded value is the bottom-left.

solved.title: Top View of Binary Tree
solved.statement: Print the nodes visible when the tree is viewed from directly above, left to right by horizontal distance.

boxes.body: `putIfAbsent` keeps only the first (topmost) BFS visit for each horizontal distance.

solved.title: Bottom View of Binary Tree
solved.statement: Print the nodes visible when the tree is viewed from directly below, left to right by horizontal distance. Only one line differs from Top View.

boxes.body: `put` always overwrites, so the last BFS visit per horizontal distance wins — that is the bottommost node.

solved.title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
solved.statement: Return vertical order traversal: nodes grouped by column (HD), sorted by row within column, and by value within same row.

boxes.body: All nodes in a column appear (unlike Top/Bottom View which only shows one). Tie-break: same (HD, depth) nodes sorted by value. Use `TreeMap<col, TreeMap<row, PriorityQueue<val>>>`.

variations.name: Maximum Width & Distance-K (Index BFS, Parent Map)
variations.coreIdea: Two BFS variants that need extra bookkeeping: width assigns heap-style indices to nodes so null gaps are counted, and Distance-K builds a parent map first so the tree can be walked upward like an undirected graph.

boxes.body: Assign indices: root=0, left child of index i = 2i, right = 2i+1. Normalize per level (subtract first index of level) to prevent long overflow in deep trees.
Binary trees only allow downward movement. To go upward, build a parent map first. Then BFS from target treating the tree as an undirected graph (3 neighbors: left, right, parent).

boxes.body: Assign indices: root=0, left child of index i = 2i, right = 2i+1. Normalize per level (subtract first index of level) to prevent long overflow in deep trees.

variations.name: Tree Construction
variations.coreIdea: All construction problems use the **divide-and-conquer** pattern on DFS. Key insight: the root is always deterministic (first in preorder, last in postorder, maximum in max-tree, or BST property). Then recursively build left and right subtrees.

items: **Inorder position lookup**: Build a `HashMap<val, index>` for inorder array so root lookup is O(1) instead of O(n).
**Preorder root**: `preorder[preStart]` is always the root.
**Postorder root**: `postorder[postEnd]` is always the root.
**Left subtree size**: If root is at index `inRoot` in inorder, left subtree has `inRoot - inStart` nodes.
**BST from preorder**: No inorder needed. Recursively pick from preorder while value is within valid range [`min`, `max`].

solved.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
solved.statement: Given preorder and inorder traversal arrays of a binary tree with unique values, construct and return the binary tree.

items: `preorder[preStart]` = root of current subtree.
Find root in inorder array. Elements left of root in inorder = left subtree. Elements right = right subtree.
Left subtree size `leftSize = inRoot - inStart` used to advance preorder pointer.

boxes.body: The first element of any preorder range is the root. Find it in the inorder array to split left and right subtrees. Recurse. Using a HashMap makes root lookup O(1).

solved.title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal
solved.statement: Given inorder and postorder traversal arrays, construct the binary tree.

boxes.body: `postorder[postEnd]` is always the root. Find it in inorder to split subtrees. Left subtree has `inRoot - inStart` nodes.

solved.title: Maximum Binary Tree
solved.statement: Build a binary tree where the root is the maximum element, with the left subtree built from elements to its left and right subtree from elements to its right (recursively).

complexity.timeNote: worst case (sorted array); O(n log n) average

solved.title: Construct Binary Search Tree from Preorder Traversal
solved.statement: Given preorder traversal of a BST, reconstruct it.

boxes.body: BST property: all left subtree values are less than root, all right subtree values are greater. In preorder, first element is root. Pass valid range [min, max] to each recursive call; consume preorder elements as long as they fall in range.

solved.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
solved.statement: Convert a sorted array to a height-balanced BST.

boxes.body: Recursively pick the middle element of the current range as the root. This guarantees height-balance because left and right subtrees have nearly equal size.

variations.name: Height-Related Problems
variations.coreIdea: Height problems use DFS. The key pattern: compute something from left and right subtrees, use it to update a global answer, then return a different (simpler) value to the parent.

solved.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
solved.statement: Return the maximum depth of the binary tree.

solved.title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
solved.statement: Minimum depth = shortest path from root to the nearest leaf node. A leaf has no children.

boxes.body: Cannot simply return `1 + min(left, right)` because if one child is null, that side is not a valid path to a leaf. Must handle the case where one subtree is missing.

solved.title: Balanced Binary Tree
solved.statement: A tree is height-balanced if for every node, the height of left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.

boxes.body: Naive: O(n^2) by computing height at each node separately. Optimal: single-pass DFS that returns -1 if unbalanced, or actual height if balanced.

bruteForce.approach: Compute height at each node separately while checking balance.

optimal.approach: Single-pass DFS using -1 as an "unbalanced" sentinel.

solved.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
solved.statement: Diameter = length of the longest path between any two nodes (path may not pass through root). Length = number of edges.

boxes.body: The longest path through a node = left height + right height. But the longest path in the tree may not pass through the root. So maintain a global max updated at every node.
DFS computes height. At each node, the longest path through that node = leftHeight + rightHeight. Update global answer. Return height to parent. Global answer after full traversal is the diameter.

variations.name: Root-to-Leaf Path Problems
variations.coreIdea: All root-to-leaf problems use DFS with a running state (current path, current sum, current XOR bitmask). At a leaf, evaluate the accumulated state. Backtrack after returning from a recursive call.

items: **Leaf detection**: `node.left == null && node.right == null`.
**Backtracking**: After adding to a list/state, recurse, then remove to backtrack.
**Passing sum down**: For path sum problems, pass `remaining = target - node.val` downward. At leaf, check if remaining == 0.
**XOR bitmask for digits**: XOR accumulates which digits appear an odd number of times. Pseudo-palindromic ⇔ `bitmask == 0` or exactly one bit set: `(bitmask & (bitmask-1)) == 0`.
**Max Path Sum**: Return the best single-arm to parent; update global with both arms combined.

solved.statement: Return all root-to-leaf paths as strings in the format "1->2->5".

complexity.space: O(h) recursion + O(n*h) for path strings

solved.title: Path Sum II
solved.statement: Return all root-to-leaf paths where the sum of node values equals targetSum.

complexity.space: O(h) recursion + O(n) for paths stored

solved.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
solved.statement: Each root-to-leaf path represents a number (digits from root to leaf). Return the total sum of all such numbers.

solved.title: Pseudo-Palindromic Paths in a Binary Tree
solved.statement: Count paths from root to leaf whose digit sequence can be rearranged into a palindrome.

boxes.body: A sequence can form a palindrome iff at most one digit appears an odd number of times. XOR-ing a digit's bit into a bitmask tracks parity. At a leaf, check if bitmask has at most one bit set: `bitmask == 0 || (bitmask & (bitmask-1)) == 0`.

solved.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
solved.statement: A path can start and end at any node. Return the maximum sum of any such path.

items: The path through a node can use left arm + node + right arm.
But returning to parent, we can only extend one arm (left or right), not both.
So: update global with (left + node + right), but return to parent max(node, node + left, node + right). Negative arms should be ignored (clamped to 0).

solved.title: Insufficient Nodes in Root to Leaf Paths
solved.statement: Remove all nodes where every root-to-leaf path through that node has a sum less than `limit`.

variations.name: Ancestor Problems
variations.coreIdea: LCA is the most important ancestor pattern. The key insight: if both target nodes exist in the tree, the LCA is the node where the search paths from root to each target first diverge.

items: **LCA base cases**: If `node == null` return null. If `node == p || node == q` return node.
**LCA combination**: If left and right both return non-null, current node is the LCA. If only one side is non-null, return that side (the answer is deeper there).
**BST LCA**: Exploit BST property — if both p and q are less than root, go left. If both are greater, go right. Otherwise, root is LCA.
**Max difference from ancestor**: Track max and min seen so far on the path from root to current node.
**Kth Ancestor**: Binary lifting (sparse table) for O(log n) per query when many queries are needed.

solved.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
solved.statement: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes p and q in a binary tree.

items: If current node is null, p, or q: return current node.
Recurse left and right.
If both return non-null: current node is the LCA.
If only one returns non-null: both p and q are in that subtree; pass the result up.

solved.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
solved.statement: Find LCA of two nodes in a BST. All node values are unique.

boxes.body: BST property allows us to decide direction without exploring both subtrees. If both p and q are smaller than root, LCA is in left subtree. If both are larger, it is in right subtree. Otherwise, root is the LCA.

solved.title: Maximum Difference Between Node and Ancestor
solved.statement: Find the maximum value of `|a - b|` where a is an ancestor of b.

boxes.body: The maximum absolute difference between any ancestor and a descendant on the same path equals the maximum of (current node value - path minimum) and (path maximum - current node value). Track both min and max on the path from root to current node.

solved.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of Deepest Leaves
solved.statement: Return the LCA of the deepest leaves. If there are multiple deepest leaves, return their LCA.

boxes.body: DFS returning a pair: (LCA candidate, depth). At each node, get (left LCA, left depth) and (right LCA, right depth). If left depth == right depth, current node is the LCA of the deepest leaves in both subtrees. Otherwise, return the deeper side's LCA.

solved.title: Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node (Binary Lifting)
solved.statement: Given a tree with n nodes and multiple queries (node, k), return the kth ancestor of node. Return -1 if no such ancestor.

boxes.body: Naive: walk up k steps per query = O(nk) total. Binary Lifting (Sparse Table): precompute `up[node][j]` = 2^j-th ancestor of node. Then answer each query in O(log k) by decomposing k into powers of 2.

bruteForce.approach: Walk up k steps per query.

complexity.time: O(n log n) precompute, O(log k) per query

variations.name: Binary Search Tree (BST)
variations.coreIdea: BST's defining property: for every node, all left descendants are smaller and all right descendants are larger. The key insight: **inorder traversal of a BST gives a sorted sequence**. Most BST problems exploit this.

items: **Validate**: Pass valid range [min, max] down. At each node, check `min < node.val < max`.
**Search/Insert**: BST property lets you decide left or right at each step without exploring both subtrees. O(h) per operation.
**Inorder for sorted order**: Any problem needing "kth smallest/largest" or "minimum difference between any two nodes" reduces to inorder traversal.
**LCA in BST**: No need for general LCA algorithm. Split point (one value left, one value right) is the LCA. O(h) not O(n).
**Range queries**: In-order traversal bounded by [low, high] skipping irrelevant subtrees.

solved.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
solved.statement: Determine if a given binary tree is a valid BST.

boxes.body: Checking only immediate children is insufficient: a node in the right subtree of the root must be greater than the root, not just its direct parent. Pass the valid range [min, max] top-down.

solved.title: Range Sum of BST
solved.statement: Return the sum of all node values in the BST that fall within [low, high].

boxes.body: BST property lets us prune: if `node.val < low`, the left subtree is entirely out of range; if `node.val > high`, the right subtree is entirely out of range.

complexity.time: O(n) worst case, O(h + k) average

solved.title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
solved.statement: Find the minimum absolute difference between values of any two nodes in a BST.

boxes.body: Inorder traversal of BST gives sorted sequence. Minimum difference between any two BST nodes must be between adjacent nodes in the inorder sequence. Track previous inorder node.

solved.title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
solved.statement: Insert a value into a BST and return the root of the modified tree.

solved.title: Delete Node in a BST
solved.statement: Delete a node with a given key from a BST and return the updated root.

boxes.body: Three cases: (1) Node is a leaf: delete directly. (2) Node has one child: replace with that child. (3) Node has two children: replace node's value with inorder successor (leftmost of right subtree), then delete the inorder successor from right subtree.

solved.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
solved.statement: Return the kth smallest value in a BST.

boxes.body: Inorder traversal of BST visits nodes in ascending order. The kth node visited is the kth smallest.

solved.title: Convert BST to Greater Tree
solved.statement: Transform a BST so that each node's value becomes the sum of all values greater than or equal to it.

boxes.body: Reverse inorder traversal (right → root → left) visits nodes in descending order. Maintain a running suffix sum and assign it to each node.

solved.title: Recover Binary Search Tree
solved.statement: Exactly two nodes of a BST are swapped by mistake. Recover the tree without changing its structure.

boxes.body: In a correct BST, inorder gives sorted sequence. With two nodes swapped, we will see at most two *inversions* (places where `prev.val >= current.val`). The first node to swap is `prev` at the first inversion; the second node is `current` at the last inversion.

variations.name: Tree DP (Dynamic Programming on Trees)
variations.coreIdea: Tree DP is the highest-difficulty and highest-differentiator pattern. At each node, compute an optimal decision based on children's results. There are usually two states per node: "include this node" and "exclude this node." The parent's choices are constrained by the child's decision.

items: **Two return values**: DFS typically returns `int[2]` or a pair: `[include, exclude]` or `[selected, notSelected]`.
**Parent-child constraint**: If a node is *included*, its children must be *excluded* (and vice versa, for problems like House Robber and Cameras).
**Greedy postorder for cameras**: Place camera at leaf's parent (not leaf). This greedy insight combined with DFS solves LC 968 optimally.
**Coins/distribution**: Think about how many coins need to flow through each edge. The cost = sum of absolute flows across all edges.

solved.title: House Robber III
solved.statement: Rob houses arranged in a binary tree. Cannot rob two directly connected houses. Return the maximum money robable.

items: For each node: two choices: rob it (cannot rob children) or skip it (children can be robbed or skipped optimally).
DFS returns `int[2]`: [maxIfRobbed, maxIfNotRobbed].
If current is robbed: gain node.val + (left NOT robbed) + (right NOT robbed).
If current is not robbed: max(left robbed, left not robbed) + max(right robbed, right not robbed).

solved.title: Binary Tree Cameras
solved.statement: Place the minimum number of cameras in a binary tree to cover all nodes. A camera at a node covers its parent, itself, and its children.

items: Three states per node: 0 = not covered, 1 = has camera, 2 = covered (by child).
Greedy insight: never place a camera at a leaf. Place cameras as high as possible (at leaf's parent). This minimizes total cameras.
Postorder DFS: if a child is in state 0 (not covered), the current node must have a camera. If any child has a camera (state 1), current node is covered (state 2).

solved.title: Distribute Coins in Binary Tree
solved.statement: Each node has some coins, total coins = total nodes. Redistribute so each node has exactly 1 coin, moving one coin per edge per move. Return minimum moves.

items: The number of moves = total coins flowing through each edge.
Excess at a subtree = (sum of coins in subtree) - (number of nodes in subtree). Excess flows through the edge connecting subtree to parent.
DFS returns excess of each subtree. Moves += |excess| for each subtree.

solved.title: Longest ZigZag Path in a Binary Tree
solved.statement: A zigzag path alternates between going left and right. Return the length of the longest such path (number of edges).

boxes.body: DFS passes direction and current length. At each node, if we came from left, we try to go right next (and continue the zigzag), or restart going left. The maximum at each node is the answer candidate.

solved.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
solved.statement: A node X is *good* if no node on the path from root to X has a value greater than X. Count good nodes.

variations.name: Serialize / Deserialize & Tree Modification
variations.coreIdea: Serialization converts a tree to a string so it can be stored or transmitted. Deserialization reconstructs the tree. The key design choice: how to represent null nodes to make the format unambiguous. Modification problems restructure the tree in place instead.

items: **Preorder with nulls**: Serialize using preorder DFS, writing "null" for missing children. Deserialize by consuming the preorder sequence: first value is root, then build left, then right.
**Use a global index**: During deserialization, use an `int[]{index}` or wrap index in an object to advance through the token array across recursive calls.
**BST optimization**: For BST, inorder gives sorted sequence so you can reconstruct without storing nulls (like LC 449).
**BFS serialization**: Level order with nulls. Intuitive but slightly more complex to deserialize.

problems.title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List

solved.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
solved.statement: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string and deserialize that string back to the original tree.

boxes.body: Preorder traversal with explicit null markers creates an unambiguous encoding. Given the preorder sequence with nulls, we can uniquely reconstruct the tree because: the first non-null is always the root, followed by its left subtree, followed by its right subtree.

solved.title: Serialize and Deserialize BST
solved.statement: More efficient serialization using BST property: no need to store null markers.

boxes.body: Preorder traversal of BST gives enough information to reconstruct it (same as LC 1008). No nulls needed since BST property determines where each element goes.

solved.title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
solved.statement: Flatten a binary tree into a linked list in-place using preorder traversal order. Right pointers link nodes; left pointers are all null.

boxes.body: Postorder approach: flatten right subtree, then left subtree. Connect left's tail to right subtree. Move left to right, set left to null.

solved.title: Trim a Binary Search Tree
solved.statement: Given a BST and range [low, high], trim the tree so all node values are within this range. Return the new root.
